prompt: `report.go` has `n := uint(r.lines)` followed by `if n >= 0 { return float64(r.errors) / float64(n) }`, and staticcheck reports `SA4003`. What does `ErrorShare` return for an empty log?
hint: Ask what `>= 0` excludes for an unsigned number, and what Go does with 0.0 / 0.0.

choices.text: Zero, from the `return 0` below the `if`
choices.why: That line is never reached: every `uint` is `>= 0`, which is exactly what `SA4003` says.

choices.text: `NaN`
choices.why: Right. The guard guards nothing, so it divides 0.0 by 0.0, and floating-point division by zero returns `NaN` in Go instead of panicking.

choices.text: It panics with `integer divide by zero`
choices.why: Both operands were converted to `float64` first; only integer division by zero panics.

choices.text: It does not compile, because staticcheck found a bug
choices.why: staticcheck reads code that already compiles, and its findings never stop `go build`.

prompt: Match each finding staticcheck printed for `report.go` with the family its check belongs to.
hint: The letters before the digits name the family.

pairs.left: `SA4003`: every value of type uint is >= 0
pairs.right: code that is wrong, or very likely to be
a shorter way to say the same thing

pairs.left: `ST1005`: error strings should not be capitalized
pairs.right: a convention the Go project writes down

right_distractors: a data race between two goroutines

prompt: Ana puts `//lint:ignore S1003 a loop over paths` on the line above `for path, n := range s.ByPath {`. The `strings.Index` it is meant to excuse is on the `if` inside the loop. What does staticcheck print?
hint: How many lines does one directive cover?

choices.text: Nothing about `S1003`: the directive covers the whole loop
choices.why: It covers one line, the `for`, and the finding is two lines below it.

choices.text: An error, because a directive inside a function is not allowed
choices.why: Directives work anywhere; the `U1000` one above `func percent` worked, and placement inside a function body is legal too.

choices.text: Both the `S1003` finding and a warning that the directive matched nothing
choices.why: Right. The directive excused nothing on its own line, so staticcheck reports it as `didn't match anything; should it be removed?`, and `S1003` still prints.

choices.text: The `S1003` finding only; an unused directive is ignored
choices.why: staticcheck reports a directive that matched nothing, so a stale one cannot linger unnoticed.

prompt: A `staticcheck.conf` line that keeps the checks the parent directory chose and switches on `ST1003` as well reads `checks = ["___", "ST1003"]`.
hint: The word means: whatever was in force above.

prompt: A CI step runs `revive ./...` with no flags and no configuration file. revive prints four findings. What does the step report?
hint: Look at revive's two exit codes in its defaults.

choices.text: Failure, since any finding is exit status 1
choices.why: That is what `staticcheck` and `golangci-lint` do. revive exited 0 with four findings printed.

choices.text: Success, with the four findings left in the log
choices.why: Right. Its defaults set `error-code` and `warning-code` to 0, so only `-set_exit_status` or a configuration file makes it fail.

choices.text: Failure, but only for the `exported` finding
choices.why: No default rule is an error, and even an error is exit 0 while `error-code` is 0.

choices.text: Nothing: revive refuses to run without `revive.toml`
choices.why: With no file it applies its 23 default rules; it found four things that way.

prompt: A team's `revive.toml` holds the global settings and one table, `[rule.unhandled-error]`, and no `enable-default-rules`. On `report.go`, which rules run?
hint: Naming a rule changes what happens to the ones not named.

choices.text: `unhandled-error` and nothing else
choices.why: Right. Naming any rule switches off every default not named; `exported`, `error-strings` and the rest stop running without a word.

choices.text: The 23 defaults, with `unhandled-error` added on top
choices.why: That is what `enable-default-rules = true` gives; without it the file means exactly the rules it names.

choices.text: All 105 rules, because a table was given
choices.why: That would be `enable-all-rules = true`, a separate setting.

choices.text: None: revive reports the missing defaults as an error
choices.why: The file is valid and revive runs it; the defaults simply are not part of it.

prompt: `[rule.unhandled-error]` has `arguments = ['^fmt\.Fprint']`, and revive still reports `Unhandled error in call to function fmt.Fprintf`. Why?
hint: The expression is compared with the function's name in a particular way.

choices.text: The arguments of a rule are ignored unless its severity is set
choices.why: Severity and arguments are independent; the rule read the argument and found that it did not match.

choices.text: The match must cover the whole name
choices.why: Right. `^fmt\.Fprint` matches only the start of `fmt.Fprintf`; the file in section 03 writes `'^fmt\.Fprint(f|ln)?$'`.

choices.text: TOML strings in single quotes are not regular expressions
choices.why: Single quotes are TOML's literal strings, which is why the backslash survives; the expression is read as written.

choices.text: `fmt` functions cannot be excused, because their errors are always real
choices.why: The rule excuses whatever its list matches; section 03's configuration lets off all three `fmt.Fprint` forms.

prompt: With section 03's `revive.toml`, the run on `~/lint` exits 1 because of `context-as-argument` and `unhandled-error`, while `exported` only prints. Which settings in the file produce that split? Choose all that apply.
hint: One setting raises two rules; two decide what each severity is worth.

choices.text: `severity = "error"` on those two rules
choices.why: Yes. It raises them above the global `severity = "warning"` that `exported` keeps.

choices.text: `error-code = 1`
choices.why: Yes. It is the exit code when the worst finding is an error.

choices.text: `warning-code = 0`
choices.why: Yes. Warnings still print and the run still passes, which is why `exported` alone would not fail it.

choices.text: `confidence = 0.8`
choices.why: Confidence filters out findings a rule is unsure of; it has nothing to do with exit codes.

choices.text: `exclude = ["TEST"]`
choices.why: That keeps `cognitive-complexity` away from test files and touches neither rule.

prompt: `golangci-lint run --no-config` on `~/lint` reported 16 issues. How many of them came from `errcheck`?
hint: Look at the summary under the list.

prompt: staticcheck run alone printed two `ST1005` lines for line 45 of `report.go`; `golangci-lint run --no-config` printed one. Where did the other go?
hint: It is a default of the output, not of the linter.

choices.text: golangci-lint's staticcheck is older and lacks half of `ST1005`
choices.why: It is v0.8.1 against v0.8.2, but with `uniq-by-line: false` both messages come back, so the check found both.

choices.text: `max-same-issues` hid it as a repeat
choices.why: That cap is three findings with the same text, and the two messages differ.

choices.text: By default golangci-lint keeps one finding per line
choices.why: Right. `uniq-by-line` is true by default; section 04's file sets it to false and both `ST1005` lines return, beside revive's on the same line.

choices.text: The `comments` preset excludes style messages
choices.why: No preset was enabled in that run: `--no-config` reads no file at all.

prompt: A colleague copies an old `.golangci.yml` that starts with `linters:` and has no `version` key, and runs golangci-lint 2.14.0. What happens?
hint: Version 2 of the tool expects a version 2 file.

choices.text: It runs the standard set and ignores the file
choices.why: An unknown key is ignored; a file with no version is refused before anything runs.

choices.text: It refuses with `unsupported version of the configuration` and exits 3
choices.why: Right. The message points at the migration guide, and `golangci-lint migrate` converts a version 1 file.

choices.text: It converts the file to version 2 in place
choices.why: Conversion is a separate command, `golangci-lint migrate`; `run` never rewrites the configuration.

choices.text: It treats the file as version 2 and reads it
choices.why: Without the key the version is empty, and golangci-lint 2 says so instead of guessing.

prompt: With section 04's `.golangci.yml` (`nolintlint` with `require-specific` and `require-explanation`), somebody ends the `os.WriteFile` line with a bare `//nolint` to get a build green. What does `golangci-lint run` report about that line?
hint: Two linters had something to say about it before; one of them still does.

choices.text: Nothing: the bare directive silences every linter on the line
choices.why: It silences the linters it covers, and `nolintlint` reports the directive itself; that is what it is for.

choices.text: The `errcheck` finding, because a directive without a reason is ignored
choices.why: The bare `//nolint` did hide `errcheck`; the missing name and reason are reported, not used to cancel the directive.

choices.text: Both the `errcheck` finding and a `nolintlint` finding
choices.why: The `errcheck` line at column 14 disappeared from the output; only the directive was reported.

choices.text: One complaint, about the directive itself
choices.why: Right. `directive //nolint should mention specific linter`, while the dropped error it hid is gone from the list.

prompt: Put in order the steps for rolling golangci-lint out on an old codebase.
hint: Report before gating, and gate new code before old.
items: start from `default: standard` and the `std-error-handling` preset
run it in CI with `--issues-exit-code=0` and read what it says
fix the cheap findings, exclude the wrong ones, and turn on `--new-from-merge-base`
pay down the old findings package by package until the flag can come off
add further linters one at a time, each with a change that makes the code pass

prompt: After the baseline commit, `share.go` is added and `golangci-lint run` reports 12 issues, while `golangci-lint run --new-from-rev=HEAD` reports 1. What did the flag do?
hint: Compare with what the commit already contained.

choices.text: Ran only the linters that changed since `HEAD`
choices.why: The set of linters is the same in both runs; what differs is which findings are kept.

choices.text: Kept only findings on lines that differ from that commit
choices.why: Right. The eleven in `report.go` sit on committed lines, and the `S1002` in `share.go` is on new ones.

choices.text: Linted only the files Git does not track yet, and skipped every committed one
choices.why: It works on changed lines in any file; on the branch, `--new-from-merge-base` gave the same answer with `share.go` committed.

choices.text: Fixed the eleven old findings automatically
choices.why: Nothing was fixed; they are still in `report.go`, filtered out of the report.

prompt: A pull request deletes the only call to an old exported-nowhere helper, leaving the helper's definition untouched. CI runs `golangci-lint run --new-from-merge-base=origin/main`. Does `unused` stop the merge?
hint: Where is `unused` reported, and which lines does the flag keep?

choices.text: Yes, because `unused` analyses the whole package and reports whatever it finds in it
choices.why: It does analyse the whole package, and then the flag drops every finding on a line the change did not touch.

choices.text: Yes, because a deleted line counts as changed
choices.why: The finding is placed on the function's definition, which the change left alone, not on the deleted call.

choices.text: No: the finding lands on an old line and is filtered out
choices.why: Right. That is the blind spot of keeping findings by changed line, and why the old pile has to shrink until the flag can come off.

choices.text: No, because `unused` is not in the standard set
choices.why: It is one of the five, alongside `errcheck`, `govet`, `ineffassign` and `staticcheck`.

prompt: Section 04's `std-error-handling` preset also silenced `genlog`'s `defer w.Flush()`. What can that cost?
hint: What does `Flush` write, and what happens to its error now?

choices.text: Nothing: `Flush` cannot fail on a `bufio.Writer`
choices.why: `Flush` writes the buffered bytes to the file underneath, and that write can fail like any other.

choices.text: A panic at the end of every run
choices.why: A dropped error is silent; nothing panics, and that is the trouble.

choices.text: A truncated log on a full disk, with `genlog` exiting 0
choices.why: Right. The last buffered lines never reach the file and nobody is told. A preset is a trade, made on purpose for eight lines of noise.

choices.text: A slower log, since the buffer is never emptied
choices.why: The `defer` still runs `Flush`; only its error is thrown away.

prompt: On a pull request, the flag that keeps only findings on lines changed since the branch left `main` is `golangci-lint run --new-from-___=main`.
hint: It names the commit Git finds with the command of the same name.

prompt: Why does section 05 pin `version: v2.14.0` in the workflow rather than ask for the latest golangci-lint?
hint: What else changes when golangci-lint changes?

choices.text: Releases change the bundled linters, and with them what is reported
choices.why: Right. 2.14.0 alone moved revive from 1.15.0 to 1.17.0 and switched `gosec`'s `G407` back on; a pin turns that into a pull request of its own.

choices.text: The action refuses to run without an exact version
choices.why: golangci-lint's own workflow passes `version: latest` to the same action.

choices.text: Newer releases need a newer Go
choices.why: That may happen, but the reason given is that findings move between releases with no change to the code.

choices.text: Pinning makes the cache work
choices.why: The cache has nothing to do with the version the workflow names; the reason is findings that move between releases.
